title: Mini-Sermonizing Academic Integrity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart shares a classroom case study from Dr. Carolyn Ross, who addressed a mid-year academic dishonesty wave in her high school English class using an approach that mirrors his Mini-Sermon methodology. Rather than confronting individual offenders or issuing threats, Ross reoriented the whole class around the intrinsic goals students had set at the start of the year, openly listed the honest reasons people cut corners, and offered grace rather than judgment. Stuart analyzes Ross’s moves through the lens of his Will to Learn methodology: she employed Valued Within (reconnecting students to their own goals), Define Success: Wisely, Early, Often, and Woodenization (breaking down the decision-points around cheating with crystal clarity). The student response—laughter, emotional visibility, and one comment calling it ‘inspiring’—illustrates the power of meeting academic dishonesty with transparency and re-centering rather than punishment.
points: When academic dishonesty becomes widespread, it is often a systems-level problem—a mid-year motivational slump—rather than an individual integrity failure; identifying it as systemic changes how a teacher responds and what interventions are appropriate.

Re-centering students on their own intrinsic goals (becoming better readers, writers, thinkers) is more effective than issuing rule reminders or consequences, because it reconnects the problematic behavior to students’ own stated values.

Naming and listing the actual reasons people cheat—directly, without accusation—produces trust, recognition, and sometimes laughter: students feel seen rather than accused, which opens them to the message.

Offering grace alongside clarity on consequences keeps the relationship intact and signals that the teacher distinguishes between the behavior and the person, a distinction students respond to with visible emotion.

The combination of Valued Within, Woodenization, and Define Success strategies produces measurable affective results even in a single class period, as Ross’s students demonstrated through their reactions.
quotes: I thought there was something universal happening here related to a mid-year slump. So I set out to re-center our purpose and also clarify my expectations.

it’s natural to lose sight of those intrinsic goals as time goes on and shift to “just getting by” — trying to pass the quiz, get the homework done, etc. But working like that won’t actually improve our skills.
They seemed a little wide-eyed to see it spelled out so directly, and someone said, “No, that covers it” and we laughed.
they were visibly moved by my suggestion that above all else they give themselves some grace.

I think it built trust that I named the behaviors directly, and set us up for less strife in the future now that my expectations are super clear. They know what happens if they cheat, but they also know I won’t think they are a bad person.
I could see a number of them really benefited from being reminded that they do value improving their skills, and they want to leave this class stronger readers, writers, and thinkers.
